passages.t: The king's dream and his impossible demand
passages.happening:
In the second year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar has dreams that trouble him so much that he cannot sleep (verse 1). He summons his magicians, enchanters, sorcerers and astrologers (verse 2).

They ask him to tell them the dream so they can interpret it. The king refuses. They must tell him the dream itself and its meaning, or they ‘will be cut into pieces and your houses will be reduced to rubble’ (verse 5). If they can do it, he will reward them richly (verse 6). He suspects they are stalling, and that they would make up a pleasing answer if he told them the dream (verses 8-9).

The astrologers protest that no one on earth can do this. No king has ever asked such a thing. Only the gods could tell it, ‘whose dwelling is not with mortals’ (verse 11).

The king is furious and orders that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed (verse 12). ‘So the decree went out that the wise men were to be executed, and men went to look for Daniel and his friends to execute them’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The dream comes about 603 BC, early in a reign that lasted until 562. That date sits awkwardly with the three years of training in chapter 1, and interpreters explain it in different ways: by Babylon's practice of counting a king's first part-year separately, so that the training could span parts of three years, or by supposing the stories were once told separately.

The king's experts were real classes of Babylonian scholars. They kept long collections of omens, and Mesopotamia had a whole literature of dream books listing what a given dream meant. What the king demands is outside that system. A manual could interpret a dream once it was told, but no manual could tell a man what he had dreamed. His suspicion that they would invent a pleasing answer was not unreasonable.

At verse 4 the book itself changes language. The astrologers answer the king in Aramaic, and from that point to the end of chapter 7 the book is written in Aramaic, the international language of the empires. These chapters about God's rule over the nations are written in the nations' own tongue.

The astrologers' complaint in verse 11 sets up the chapter. They say the gods do not live among mortals. The rest of the chapter will show a God who does reveal himself, through a young exile.
passages.later: The scene recalls Joseph before Pharaoh, whose ‘spirit was troubled, so he summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt’ (Genesis 41:8). Later in Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar will turn to Daniel first, saying, ‘I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you’ (Daniel 4:9).
passages.hard:
A king orders all the wise men of his realm put to death because they cannot tell his dream. How should a reader take that?

The story does not approve of the king. It shows the absolute power of an ancient ruler over his servants, and how quickly that power turned cruel when he was afraid. The threat to cut men in pieces and destroy their houses was the kind of threat such kings made. The book will spend the next four chapters humbling kings like this one.

Notice too that Daniel does not celebrate the downfall of Babylon's experts. When the moment comes, the first thing he asks is that they not be killed (verse 24). The faithful exile pleads for the lives of the very men whose learning failed.
passages.asks: The king wanted an answer no human system could give him. Ask where you are demanding certainty that no one can supply. And ask how you treat people when you are afraid.

passages.t: Daniel prays, and praises the God who reveals
passages.happening:
When Arioch, the commander of the king's guard, comes to carry out the order, ‘Daniel replied with discretion and tact’ (verse 14). He asks why the decree is so harsh, and Arioch explains (verse 15). Daniel goes in and asks the king for time (verse 16).

He goes home and tells his friends Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, urging them ‘to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery’ (verse 18), so that they would not be killed with the rest.

That night the mystery is revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he praises God (verse 19). His prayer is a small psalm. Wisdom and power belong to God. ‘He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them’ (verse 21). ‘He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him’ (verse 22). And Daniel thanks the God of his fathers for making the king's dream known (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Daniel's first move is not cleverness. It is courtesy and time. He speaks to the executioner with discretion, asks for a delay, and then gathers his friends to pray. The answer comes to a praying community, not to a lone genius.

The title the God of heaven was common for Israel's God in the Persian period, and it was used in writing meant for people of many nations. Daniel speaks of God in terms a Babylonian could understand: the God above all the gods of the city.

The word mystery, raz, probably a loanword from Persian, means something hidden that only God can reveal. The Dead Sea Scrolls use it for God's hidden purposes.

The prayer of verses 20 to 23 is the thesis of the whole book in a few lines. God changes the times. God removes kings and sets them up. God reveals what is hidden. Everything that follows in Daniel works these out. The first hearers, living under the power of other kings, were being taught to see whose hand set those kings up and took them down.
passages.later: Joseph said the same before Pharaoh: ‘I myself cannot do it,’ and that God would give the answer (Genesis 41:16). And a psalm says of the LORD, ‘darkness is as light to You’ (Psalm 139:12).
passages.asks: Daniel's first response to a crisis was to ask for time and gather people to pray. Ask what your first response usually is. And ask who you would call to pray with you if your life were on the line.

passages.t: Daniel before the king, and the dream of the statue
passages.happening:
Daniel goes to Arioch and says, ‘Do not execute the wise men of Babylon’ (verse 24), and asks to be taken to the king. Arioch hurries him in, claiming that he has found a man among the exiles who can do it (verse 25).

The king asks whether Daniel can tell him the dream and its meaning. Daniel answers that no wise man can do that, ‘But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries’ (verse 28). And he says the mystery has been revealed to him ‘not because I have more wisdom than any man alive’ (verse 30), but so the king might understand.

Then he tells the dream. A great, dazzling statue stood before the king. ‘The head of the statue was pure gold, its chest and arms were silver, its belly and thighs were bronze, its legs were iron, and its feet were part iron and part clay’ (verses 32-33). A stone was cut out, ‘but not by human hands’ (verse 34), and it struck the feet and crushed them.

The whole statue shattered and blew away like chaff. ‘But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Daniel's first words to Arioch are a plea for the other wise men. He does not take the chance to see his rivals destroyed.

Before the king, he refuses the credit twice. The God in heaven reveals mysteries, and the revelation was not given because Daniel is wiser than anyone else. The first hearers, exiles in a land that prized its own learning, heard a young man from a conquered people telling the most powerful king on earth that wisdom belongs to Israel's God.

The statue is built in descending order, from gold to silver to bronze to iron to iron mixed with clay. The metals lose value, but the iron grows harder and more violent. The stone is its opposite. It is not made by human hands, it begins small, and it becomes a mountain filling the whole earth.

A stone cut without hands is a way of saying God's own work. Kings in the ancient world set up statues of themselves and their gods. This statue is smashed by something no king made.
passages.later: Other Scripture speaks of a stone God lays: ‘See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone’ (Isaiah 28:16), and of ‘The stone the builders rejected’ (Psalm 118:22). After quoting that psalm, Jesus added, ‘Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed’ (Luke 20:18), and many interpreters hear in it an echo of the stone in this dream.
passages.asks: Daniel told the king plainly that the gift was not his own. Ask where you are tempted to take credit for what you were given. And ask what you might be building that the stone of this dream would blow away like chaff.

passages.t: Four kingdoms, and the kingdom that will never be destroyed
passages.happening:
Daniel gives the meaning. ‘You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given sovereignty, power, strength, and glory’ (verse 37). ‘You are that head of gold’ (verse 38).

After him will come another kingdom, lesser than his, then a third of bronze that will rule the whole earth (verse 39). The fourth will be as strong as iron, and it will crush all the others (verse 40). But it will be divided, partly strong and partly brittle, and its peoples will mix with one another but not hold together, any more than iron mixes with clay (verses 41-43).

Then the heart of the dream: ‘In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people’ (verse 44). It will shatter the other kingdoms and stand forever.

The king falls on his face before Daniel and orders an offering presented to him (verse 46). ‘Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries’ (verse 47). He makes Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon and chief over all its wise men, and at Daniel's request he appoints Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego to manage the province (verses 48-49).
passages.hearers:
Only the head of gold is named, and it is Nebuchadnezzar. Even the great king, Daniel says, holds his power because the God of heaven gave it to him. The first hearers, under that king's rule or his successors', heard that every empire is on loan.

The word for kingdom, malkhu, is used for the kingdoms of the statue and for the kingdom God sets up. God's rule is not a feeling or an idea. It is a real kingdom, and it competes with the others and outlasts them.

The chapter ends with a pattern that will come back in chapters 3, 4 and 6: a pagan king confessing that Israel's God is above all gods. The king's homage to Daniel goes further than Daniel asked, and the text records it without comment. Daniel uses his new place to bring his friends into office, which sets up the test of the next chapter.
passages.later: Chapter 7 returns to the same four kingdoms as four beasts, with God's kingdom given to ‘One like the Son of Man’ (Daniel 7:13). Jesus began his preaching by announcing that ‘the kingdom of God is near’ (Mark 1:15). And Revelation hears loud voices in heaven say, ‘The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ’ (Revelation 11:15).
passages.hard:
Which four kingdoms does the statue stand for?

The head of gold is named: it is Nebuchadnezzar (verse 38). The rest are not named in this chapter. The traditional Christian reading, found in Jerome and held by many today, takes them as Media-Persia (silver), Greece (bronze) and Rome (iron), with the stone as the kingdom of God coming in Christ in the Roman period. Most critical scholars, and some others, read them as Media, Persia and Greece, with the iron mixed with clay as the divided Greek kingdoms of the Ptolemies and Seleucids, whose attempts to unite by royal marriages failed (compare verse 43 with 11:6, 17). Supporters of that reading note that Daniel treats the Medes as a kingdom before Persia (5:31; 6:28). Supporters of the first note that 8:20 joins Media and Persia in a single ram. Some futurist readers add that the iron kingdom reaches into a revived form at the end of history.

These notes take no side, and they name no nation of the present day as any part of the statue. All the readings agree on the point the chapter makes most plainly: every human kingdom is temporary, and God's kingdom will replace them all.
passages.asks: The king of kings was told his gold was on loan from God. Ask what power or position you hold that you treat as your own. And ask what it would change to live as a citizen of the kingdom that will never be destroyed, while serving faithfully in the kingdoms that will.
